title: CSS selectors cannot reliably identify cells on the edge of their containing table if any cells in the table use the rowSpan attribute
body:
Currently, there is no way for CSS to reliably identify when a table cell is the bottommost cell in its column, or the leftmost cell in its row. If any cells in the table use, or may use, `rowSpan`, then there is no longer any way for CSS to know. Typically, we'd be able to tell if a cell touches a given edge of the table as follows: ```css /* Top edge: */ table > :is(thead,tbody,tfoot):first-child > tr:first-child > :is(td,th) {} /* Bottom edge: */ table > :is(thead,tbody,tfoot):last-child > tr:last-child > :is(td,th) {} /* Left edge: */ table > :is(thead,tbody,tfoot) > tr > :is(td,th):first-child {} /* Right edge: */ table > :is(thead,tbody,tfoot) > tr > :is(td,th):last-child {} ``` These checks break down when `rowSpan` enters the picture. Consider: ```html
A B
C
``` We cannot here tell that A touches the bottom of the table, or that C *doesn't* touch the left edge of the table, through CSS alone. (We could write CSS specifically for *this* table with *this* arrangement of cells, but styles intended for tables with arbitrary layouts have no way to cope with the use of `rowSpan` here.) ## Use cases for this **Tables with rounded corners.** Applying `border-radius` to a table with separated borders won't actually round off the corners on its corner cells; cells are drawn overtop the table and retain their rectangular edges. This means that if you want a table with rounded corners, you need to manually select the corner cells in CSS and enable the matching `border-radius` values. For example, the cell in the bottom-left corner must have `border-bottom-left-radius` set. Per the above, however, you cannot reliably identify that cell in tables that may use `rowSpan`. **Tables with rounded corners *and* collapsing borders.** Setting `border-collapse: collapse` on a table will forcibly disable `border-radius`. This means that to have a table with rounded corners and collapsing borders, you must leave `border-collapse` off, do all of the above, and additionally emulate the effect of `border-collapse` by selectively hiding table cells' borders. Given any two adjacent cells, one cell must have its border on the shared edge hidden; given a cell at an edge of the table, the cell must have the border on that edge hidden. Per the above, however, you cannot reliably tell when a cell shares its left edge with the right edge of a rowspanned cell from a previous row; you also can't tell when a rowspanned cell shares its bottom edge with the bottom edge of its containing table. Using our example above, we can't set a bottom-left border radius on cell A; we can't know *not* to set a bottom-left border radius on cell C; and we can't hide the left-side border on cell C in order to collapse it into A's right-side border. I've written [an article](https://davidjcobb.github.io/articles/css-rowspan-issue) going over this three-way conflict between `border-collapse`, `border-radius`, and `rowSpan`, with visual examples. **Tables with visually collapsing borders, but which use any other effect that requires separated borders under the hood.** For example, if you want a table to have collapsing borders between cells, but you also want the table itself to have a multi-layered border, e.g. * A 1px black border * A 3px grey border * A 1px dark grey border then the easiest way to achieve that (without any extra elements such as wrappers, anyway) would be by: * Using separated borders * Giving the table a 1px black border * Giving the table a 3px padding with a grey background color * Giving cells along any edge of the table a 1px dark grey border along that edge (i.e. instead of hiding these borders and emulating the cell borders collapsing into the table borders) The general table styles for my site (outside of the article linked above) have this design. There's an article on my site that has styled tables with rowspanned cells, [here](https://davidjcobb.github.io/articles/multinomial-theorem); you can DOM inspect those and see how I've had to use a `force-is-bottom-row` class on a bottom-left rowspanned cell, and a `force-is-not-leftmost` class on the cells adjacent to it. ## Potential solutions One can manually add CSS classes to tables that are known to rest or not rest on a given edge, in order to forcibly mark them as edge cells when selectors wouldn't see them, or forcibly mark them as *not* edge cells when selectors would false-positive on them. For especially complex tables with strange arrangements of `rowSpan` and `colSpan` values, this may require trial and error. This is also arguably a violation of separation of concerns -- codifying style information into the markup. One can write JavaScript to scan through a table and automatically annotate cells as necessary. For especially complex tables with strange arrangements of `rowSpan` and `colSpan` values, this will fail, unless the JavaScript one writes accurately reimplements the same layout logic re: those attributes as the browser itself. This is also a violation of separation of concerns -- codifying style information into page behavior. In terms of potentially adding things to the spec to deal with this, the only idea I can think of is CSS pseudo-classes which would select cells on any given edge of their containing table, e.g. `td:table-left-edge` or `td:table-edge(left)` or `td:table-edge(inline-start)`.
